subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: During the fight-or-flight response, which branch of the nervous system is activated first?
questions.explain: The sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system triggers the acute fight-or-flight arousal response.

questions.q: In Sperry's split-brain studies, an object shown to the right visual field could be named because it was processed by the:
questions.explain: The right visual field projects to the left hemisphere, which contains the language centres, so the object could be named.

questions.q: Which gland is often called the 'master gland' because it controls the release of hormones from other glands?
questions.explain: The pituitary gland is the master gland, regulating hormone release from other endocrine glands throughout the body.

questions.q: In split-brain patients, an object presented to the left visual field could not be named because:
options: The image never reached the brain
The right hemisphere processed it but lacks language centres
questions.explain: The left visual field projects to the right hemisphere, which lacks language production, so the object could not be verbally named.

questions.q: Sperry's split-brain research has been criticised for:
options: Using a very large random sample
Generalising from a small, unusual sample of epileptic patients
Having no control conditions at all
questions.explain: A limitation of Sperry's work is that conclusions are based on a small, atypical sample of patients with severe epilepsy.

questions.q: The peripheral nervous system is divided into the somatic nervous system and the:
questions.explain: The PNS comprises the somatic nervous system (voluntary movement) and the autonomic nervous system (involuntary functions).

questions.q: After a stressful event has passed, the body returns to its resting state through activation of the:
questions.explain: The parasympathetic branch acts as a brake, returning the body to rest-and-digest after the threat has passed.

questions.q: The function of the myelin sheath on an axon is to:
options: Speed up the transmission of the electrical impulse
questions.explain: The fatty myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds up electrical transmission via saltatory conduction.

questions.q: The hormone released by the pineal gland that helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle in response to darkness is:
questions.explain: Melatonin, secreted by the pineal gland in response to darkness, promotes sleep and helps regulate circadian rhythms.

questions.q: fMRI measures brain activity by detecting changes in:
options: Blood oxygenation and flow (the haemodynamic response)
questions.explain: fMRI detects the haemodynamic response, measuring changes in blood-oxygen levels and flow associated with neural activity.

questions.q: In Sperry's split-brain research, the corpus callosum of participants had been:
questions.explain: Sperry studied patients whose corpus callosum had been cut to treat epilepsy, preventing communication between hemispheres.

questions.q: A key strength of fMRI compared with EEG is its:
options: Ability to record from the scalp
questions.explain: fMRI has high spatial resolution, providing detailed images of which brain regions are active, though its temporal resolution is poorer.

questions.q: An excitatory neurotransmitter such as adrenaline acting on a postsynaptic neuron will:
questions.explain: Excitatory neurotransmitters make the postsynaptic neuron more positively charged, increasing the likelihood of an action potential.

questions.q: During synaptic transmission, neurotransmitters are released from the presynaptic neuron and cross the:
questions.explain: Neurotransmitters diffuse across the synaptic cleft (gap) to bind with receptors on the postsynaptic neuron.

questions.q: Studies of contagion in all-female institutions, such as McClintock's work, are often cited as evidence that infradian rhythms can be influenced by:
questions.explain: Research suggesting synchronisation of menstrual cycles indicates that exogenous cues such as pheromones may influence infradian rhythms.

questions.q: In the fight-or-flight response, the adrenal medulla releases which hormone to prepare the body for action?
questions.explain: The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline, triggering physiological changes such as increased heart rate to prepare for fight or flight.

questions.q: An event-related potential (ERP) is derived from EEG data and represents:
options: The brain's averaged electrical response to a specific stimulus
questions.explain: ERPs are obtained by averaging many EEG recordings to isolate the brain's response to a specific stimulus or event.

questions.q: A limitation of post-mortem examinations as a way of studying the brain is that:
options: They have very high temporal resolution
Cause and effect cannot be confidently established and damage may have other causes
They can only be done on living participants
questions.explain: Post-mortem studies cannot establish causation and observed damage may result from factors other than the behaviour of interest.

questions.q: The endocrine system communicates by releasing chemical messengers called hormones via the:
questions.explain: The endocrine system uses glands to secrete hormones into the bloodstream, which travel to target organs.

questions.q: The process of summation in synaptic transmission refers to:
options: The total number of neurons in the brain
The net effect of excitatory and inhibitory signals on the postsynaptic neuron
questions.explain: Summation is the combined excitatory and inhibitory inputs that determine whether the postsynaptic neuron reaches its threshold and fires.

questions.q: Which type of neuron carries messages from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles?
questions.explain: Motor neurons carry signals from the CNS to effectors (muscles and glands) to produce a response.

questions.q: Plasticity of the brain refers to its ability to:
options: Change and adapt its structure and connections as a result of experience
questions.explain: Plasticity is the brain's capacity to reorganise itself by forming new neural connections in response to learning or experience.

questions.q: Functional recovery after brain trauma is an example of plasticity in which:
options: Unaffected areas take over functions of damaged areas
questions.explain: In functional recovery, healthy brain regions can take over functions previously performed by damaged areas.

questions.q: Axonal sprouting, a mechanism of functional recovery, involves:
options: The growth of new nerve endings to connect with undamaged neurons
The thickening of the myelin sheath
questions.explain: Axonal sprouting is the growth of new nerve endings that reconnect neurons whose links were damaged, aiding recovery.

questions.q: Synaptic transmission is described as unidirectional because:
options: Receptors exist on both sides equally
Neurotransmitters are released only from the presynaptic neuron and bind to the postsynaptic neuron
Neurons only exist in one part of the brain
questions.explain: Transmission is one-way because neurotransmitters are released from the presynaptic terminal and received by postsynaptic receptors only.

questions.q: Wernicke's area is mainly associated with:
questions.explain: Wernicke's area, in the left temporal lobe, is responsible for understanding language; damage causes fluent but meaningless speech.

questions.q: Maguire et al.'s study of London taxi drivers supported plasticity by finding larger volume in their:
questions.explain: Taxi drivers had a larger posterior hippocampus, linked to spatial navigation, demonstrating experience-dependent plasticity.

questions.q: The autonomic nervous system is subdivided into the sympathetic and the:
questions.explain: The autonomic nervous system has sympathetic (arousing) and parasympathetic (calming, 'rest and digest') branches.

questions.q: An exogenous zeitgeber is best described as:
options: An external environmental cue that resets biological rhythms
questions.explain: Exogenous zeitgebers are external cues, such as light, that entrain or reset internal biological rhythms.

questions.q: Lateralisation of brain function refers to the idea that:
options: Only the left hemisphere is active
Certain functions are dominant in one hemisphere
The two hemispheres are identical in function
Functions are spread evenly across both hemispheres
questions.explain: Lateralisation means that some functions, such as language, are dominant in or controlled by one hemisphere rather than both.
